text: Chapter two gave you the frameworks and operating models. Chapter three names the actual people inside them, starting with the role everything else depends on: the data owner.

DAMA-DMBOK defines a data owner as the individual responsible for definition, policy, and practice decisions about data within their area of responsibility. In practice that's four things: approving access, setting quality thresholds, resolving disputes between teams, and owning the outcome when something in their domain goes wrong.

Here's the mistake almost every organization makes the first time: handing ownership to IT by default, because IT is who technically touches the data. DAMA-DMBOK is explicit that this is backwards. A database administrator can tell you how a table is structured; only a business leader can tell you what the numbers inside it actually mean. Ownership is a named business leader's job, one owner per domain, who can delegate daily work without giving up accountability.

That delegation is exactly the relationship between owner and steward, which Lesson 17's RACI model makes precise: the owner is Accountable — the A — and the steward is Responsible — the R. Same domain, two different kinds of accountability.
One named owner, four accountabilities, and a business role IT should never default into. Next lesson: the steward who does the work the owner is accountable for. See you there.
